title: Franklin missed the Nobel not just because she died young
dek: She shot Photo 51 and was the first to see that DNA's two forms convert into each other; but what really got her underrated by history is that the King's College lab refused to share information, while Cambridge shared.
why: This is a rebroadcast from the BBC archive, medium information density, but the three guests explain Photo 51, A-form and B-form DNA, and the Nobel rules more clearly than most popular science.
who: Readers interested in the history of science, the situation of women in research, and how DNA was discovered; anyone who wants to understand how Nobel rules and lab politics shape credit allocation.
skip: The first two minutes or so are ads and show introductions for other BBC podcasts; skippable.

points.h: What Cambridge gave women was a diploma, not a degree
points.body: Franklin entered Cambridge in 1938 to read natural sciences; at the time the university capped women at 500, confined to the two women's colleges, Newnham and Girton. She sat every exam and took a first in one year, but the university did not award women degrees, only diplomas, and she never attended a graduation ceremony. Patricia Farrar points out that what was really hard was not the number of men but the attitude of "you don't belong here" — at Cambridge they were merely "a presence", not ordinary students.

points.h: She first turned coal from mysticism into something testable
points.body: In wartime, coal decided Britain's electricity and railways, but no one could say clearly why coal from different mines had different properties. Franklin used gas to probe coal's porosity and found that some pores could only admit small molecules like helium while others admitted larger ones; after heating, some coal turned into graphite, some into a glass-like "glassy carbon", the latter extremely valuable. Jim Naismith says her work let the mines predict how a coal would behave under given conditions from a sample, without having to dig it out and try it first. This was single-author work during and after her PhD, and was recognised as hers at the time.

points.h: One DNA photo took 100 hours of exposure
points.body: Judith Howard describes the equipment of the day: X-ray tubes were fairly primitive, Franklin had to clean diffusion pumps herself with buckets of benzene to maintain a vacuum, cameras were often homemade, and the sample — a lump of coal, a crystal or a fibre — had to be held by hand and aligned with the beam. Data could only be recorded on photographic film, and some of her later exposures of DNA fibres ran to about 100 hours. Today data is collected digitally, computers are fast, and instruments are made by companies, but Howard stresses this is not a different science, only a different way of doing it.

points.h: One letter planted the hostility between her and Wilkins
points.body: Franklin was hired to work on proteins, then told by a letter that she would switch to DNA, and told again that she would work with the PhD student Ray Gosling. But the message Maurice Wilkins received was that she would join his team and work under him. On her first day at King's College, Wilkins happened to be on holiday. Patricia Farrar says Franklin believed she was independently in charge and was Gosling's doctoral supervisor, while Wilkins believed she worked for him, and this mismatch was the source of every problem over the following years. The two also got on terribly in person, and Farrar judges that both were probably equally at fault.

points.h: She was shut out of the pub and the parties
points.body: Daily life at King's College was systematically isolating for Franklin: she was not allowed into the common room for lunch, and when her male colleagues went to the pub after work she could not go either, and parties did not invite her. Patricia Farrar says what is written in law is not what actually happens, and attitude is what counts. The one person always loyal was her PhD student Ray Gosling, who took the famous photograph, and who admired her greatly. Farrar warns that this kind of small daily exclusion can very quickly leave a person completely isolated.

points.h: The key to Photo 51 is B-form DNA
points.body: Jim Naismith explains that Wilkins had already taken DNA photographs, from a sample sourced in Switzerland of unprecedented quality, but the early images were complex and hard to interpret. Franklin's distinctive contribution was working out that the two forms of DNA — A-form (dehydrated, twisted, shorter) and B-form (hydrated, swollen) — could convert into each other, and Photo 51 was of the B-form. The helical structure of the B-form is very obvious, and as soon as Watson saw it and the measurements in it, he made that leap. Naismith uses the analogy of a wet towel: wring the water out and it gets shorter and twisted, that is A-form; soak it full of water and it swells, that is B-form.

points.h: She was tied to the A-form and missed the B-form helix
points.body: Jim Naismith offers an explanation opposite to the popular claim that Franklin lacked imagination: she was assigned to the A-form, Wilkins to the B-form, and Photo 51 was a B-form result that she did not give enough weight to. Add to that the King's College team's refusal to cooperate, and if everyone had seen that photograph the outcome might have been different. The A-form itself does not show clear helical features, and she worried that A only became helical when it turned into B, so she held back on the helical structure. Crick and Watson chose to ignore that distinction. She was still the first to recognise that the A and B forms could convert into each other with humidity.

points.h: The Nobel rules mean even a living Franklin might not have won
points.body: Patricia Farrar gives two technical reasons: Franklin had already died by the time the Nobel was announced, and the Nobel is only awarded to the living; and the Nobel can go to at most three people. Farrar says that if she had lived, she would like to believe the prize would have gone to Watson, Crick and Franklin. But she stresses it is hard to put a number on her contribution, because at the time information came from many directions — spectroscopy, biochemistry, different methods studying the same material, one jigsaw puzzle.

points.h: Her virus work is the signature work she did independently
points.body: After leaving King's College, Franklin went to Bernal's lab at Birkbeck to study tobacco mosaic virus. Judith Howard says the atmosphere there was completely different, and that she used the experience she had accumulated to obtain single-crystal samples and take excellent photographs. Jim Naismith adds that viruses are fascinating because they are not alive yet transmit information, and Franklin worked out how the protein coat was organised and where the nucleic acid sat inside the virus, a key question for understanding virus structure. Howard notes that across her whole shortened career, people fixate on less than two years of DNA work.

quotes.text: What mattered isn't the number of men. It's the attitudes towards the women.

So right from the very beginning, Rosalind Franklin assumed she was working on her own in charge of Ray Gosling. She was his PhD supervisor. So Wilkins chose to assume that she was working with him and for him, and that was the source of all the problems that ensued over the next few years.
And I think it also represents two different ways of approaching science. And we tend to celebrate Watson and Crick because precisely they made this imaginative leap.

She was tied to A form. This was a B form result. She didn't give it the attention that she should have done. And that team in Kings wouldn't work as a team. Had they all looked at that, it might have been different.
But I think that what was the problem was she was never given the credit at the time as to how important that image was.
I get the impression that she would have liked to be remembered not as a woman, but as a scientist who did very, very important work in DNA, in coal, in the tobacco mosaic virus.
One thing that's missed is what a kind person she was, and she made lots of friends in science.
